paragraphs.text: Immunodeficiency-35 is an autosomal recessive disorder caused by TYK2 deficiency. Kreins et al. (2015) concluded that the core clinical phenotype of complete TYK2 deficiency is mycobacterial and/or viral infections, caused by impaired responses to IL-12 and IFN-alpha/beta. They also concluded that impaired IL-6 responses and hyper-IgE syndrome (HIES) do not appear to be intrinsic features of TYK2 deficiency in humans. Wu et al. (2020) summarized the main features as normal lymphocyte counts with defects in multiple cytokine signaling pathways, susceptibility to viruses or intracellular bacteria, and IgE that may or may not be elevated.

paragraphs.text: Kilic et al. (2012) reported a Turkish boy, born to first-cousin parents, who developed disseminated BCG disease after vaccination at 2 months of age. Left axillary lymphadenopathy appeared at 8 months. By 21 months he had generalized fistulous cervical, axillary, and inguinal lymphadenopathy with fever. M. bovis BCG was isolated from discharging sinuses, and lymph node histology showed acid-fast bacilli. He recovered without relapse after 18 months of antimycobacterial therapy. At age 8 years he developed neurobrucellosis, with seizures, neck stiffness, and Brucella-positive blood and CSF cultures. It left him with severe sensorineural hearing loss, severe cognitive impairment, and lacunar infarcts on MRI. At 11 years he had herpes zoster of the maxillary branch of the trigeminal nerve, which was treated with acyclovir and did not recur.

paragraphs.text: Unlike the first reported Japanese TYK2-deficient patient, the patient of Kilic et al. (2012) had no features of hyper-IgE syndrome. He had no atopy, asthma, eczema, staphylococcal or candidal skin infections, and no skeletal or dental abnormalities. His serum IgE ranged from 80 to 218 IU/ml, which was normal or only slightly elevated. Serum IgG, IgM, and IgA levels, lymphocyte subsets, and the NBT test were normal. The authors suggested that TYK2 deficiency should be considered in patients with BCG disease or other intramacrophage infections, particularly those with severe herpesvirus infections, even in the absence of HIES features.

paragraphs.text: Zhang et al. (2022) studied an international cohort of 112 children under 16 years of age who were hospitalized for COVID-19 pneumonia. Twelve (10.7%) had recessive complete inborn errors of type I IFN immunity: XLR TLR7 deficiency (7 children) and AR deficiency of IFNAR1 (1), STAT2 (1), or TYK2 (3). None of these 15 recessive deficiencies was found in 1,224 SARS-CoV-2-infected controls without pneumonia (P = 1.2 x 10(-11)). In the 3 unrelated consanguineous Turkish children with TYK2 deficiency (P2-P4), whole-exome or whole-genome sequencing identified the same homozygous TYK2 frameshift variant, P216Rfs*14, which was confirmed by Sanger sequencing. The variant had previously been shown to cause loss of expression in patient cells, and the authors confirmed that it was loss-of-function. Eight of the 12 patients in the series were tested for autoantibodies against type I IFNs, and all were negative. The authors identified AR TYK2 deficiency as a new genetic cause of COVID-19 pneumonia.

paragraphs.text: In 3 unrelated children (P2-P4) with COVID-19 pneumonia, each born to a different set of consanguineous Turkish parents, Zhang et al. (2022) used whole-exome or whole-genome sequencing to identify a homozygous frameshift variant in the TYK2 gene (P216Rfs*14), which was confirmed by Sanger sequencing. Family segregation analysis confirmed AR inheritance. The 3-year-old younger sister of P3 had the same homozygous genotype; she had a history of critical influenza pneumonia and disseminated varicella but had not been infected with SARS-CoV-2. The variant had previously been shown to cause loss of expression in patient cells, and the authors confirmed that it was loss-of-function. ACE2-transduced SV40 fibroblasts from a homozygous patient did not control SARS-CoV-2 replication normally and failed to induce ISGs after viral infection or IFN-alpha-2b pretreatment.
